newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis edges forward as rebels free 7.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis edges forward as rebels free 7.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered the New Year on Wednesday with Marxist rebels freeing seven more captives despite President Alberto Fujimori's apparent adherence to his "no concessions" stance.
The move maintained the slow momentum in the siege negotiations following the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels' freeing of another two hostages on Tuesday.
But the rebels' gesture did little to change the overall balance in their two-week-old standoff with the government.
They still held 74 men they consider their best bargaining chips -- including two government ministers, Peruvian security force top brass, two foreign ambassadors and Japanese VIPs.

The latest release included four Japanese -- all businessmen -- and three Peruvians, including the government's key privatisation official, Juan Assereto. All of them appeared in good health as they strolled out of the Japanese ambassador's residence which the rebels stormed on Dec. 17.
Fujimori's close ally and observer at talks between the rebels and government, Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, seemed instrumental in bringing about the release.

Unlike most previous releases, the MRTA rebels did not give a reason for Wednesday's decision, but Cipriani, who accompanied the freed hostages out of the residence, said he thanked God for the decision "on this day when the church celebrates the universal day of peace."
The freeing of the hostages on Wednesday came as Fujimori refused to grab a double-edged sword offered him the day before by guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.
Cerpa told Fujimori on Tuesday "the doors of the residence are open" for government negotiator Domingo Palermo, but insisted on the release of all the rebels' roughly 400 jailed comrades.

But apparently angered at the rebels' staging a publicity coup by granting impromptu interviews inside the residence on Tuesday, Fujimori holed himself up on Wednesday in Government Palace and kept Palermo away from the compound.

Under an accord hashed out by the Red Cross, the two sides agreed journalists could cross police lines on Tuesday to film the residence close up. But the rebel leader summoned them inside the booby-trapped, mined compound.
Dressed in green military fatigues and covering his face with a red-and-white bandanna, Cerpa held court for about two hours as the rebels harangued Fujimori's "dictatorship."
Despite freeing more than 420 hostages since the crisis began, the rebels hoped to use the remaining hostages as leverage for the release of their jailed comrades.
"We are inflexible in our original position ... I do not see an immediate solution," Cerpa said.
While Fujimori refrained from sending a message to the hostages, Emperor Akihito spoke obliquely of the crisis.
"My heart hurts deeply when I think of those who cannot celebrate the New Year with their families," Akihito was quoted as saying by Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun.

Journalists who entered the Japanese compound on Tuesday described a scene like a ghost ship in the gardens of the residence. Empty bottles and discarded plates gave the residence the ironic appearance of many other post-New Year's Eve homes after Peru tried to celebrate the start of 1997.
Wary of alarming the 20-odd heavily armed rebels, Lima authorities banned the usual cacophonous celebration of the New Year with rockets and fireworks in the San Isidro neighbourhood.

Reporters and police camped outside the residence twirled a few desultory sparklers at midnight but otherwise only the occasional explosion lit up the sky, and nothing that the rebels could interpret as an armed assault.
In the morning the subdued New Year's Eve melted into one more day in captivity for the top Peruvian officials, foreign diplomats and Japanese businessmen held under the guns by their MRTA captors.
As a sign of their continuing light mood inside, Cipriani took into the compound two guitars as accompaniment for the captives' now regular singing sessions.
With the gradual release of 420 hostages, the overcrowded conditions inside the two-story mansion in the first week of the crisis have given way to a more relaxed atmosphere.
